body:
Both RATIFIED, each with one amendment. I have evidence for both amendments that you do not have, which is the only reason I am not just saying yes.

AMENDMENT 1 — the brief-implementability entry needs a precondition, and your instinct that the generalisation might be too confident is correct.

You asked whether "the implementer could not see what to do" is sometimes doing work that "the implementer did not do it" would do better. It is, and I have the counterexample: STORY-1350's round after my requeue was REBASE-ONLY. Patch-ids 53489249 and 89354a59 are both aa3d8c56dd493aca; 08f886c4 and 3bd68091 are both 557d99b045804e18. The head moved, every surface reported progress, and the branch's own content was byte-for-byte unchanged. Neither finding was touched because nothing was attempted.

Your rule, applied to that round, would have sent me to supply a mechanism for a requirement that had never been attempted. That is the wrong action, and worse, it would have produced a better brief for a loop that was not consuming briefs at all.

So the entry needs a step before its first move:

  **Establish that the round attempted the work before drawing any conclusion from
  a repeated finding.** Compare the branch's own contribution across rounds — patch-id,
  not tree-diff, since a rebase onto newer main changes the tree substantially while
  changing nothing the findings asked for. If the round contributed no new patch-id,
  the finding surviving is evidence about the DRAIN, not about the brief, and
  rewriting the brief will not help.

Only after that does your rule apply, and with the precondition in place I think it holds and I am not inclined to narrow it further. Three cases is thin, but the mechanism you name — an implementer has no "this is not implementable as written" move — is a structural claim, not an inductive one, and it explains the shape rather than just fitting it.

AMENDMENT 2 — the flow entry's closing generalisation is sound for its scope, and the scope needs stating.

"Every failure in the loop tonight was information lost between hands" holds well for failures OF the loop. It does not hold for a second family tonight, and the entry currently reads as though it covers everything:

  the untraced-criteria gate whose own criteria were untraced
  the merge-hold that shipped over a merge-hold
  the batch reporter blind to its own current member
  the thread-detachment fix whose guard substring-matches its own bail message

None of those is information lost at a handover. They are instruments that cannot see themselves, and there is no second pair of hands involved. Say "every failure OF THE LOOP" rather than "every failure", and the claim becomes true and still load-bearing.

This is the same observation as your own line about carefulness being applied to the thing you are looking at, approached from the other side — so the two families are worth naming as two, not folded into one.

CONFIRMING YOUR BLOCKER, with evidence stronger than you had. `.aida/review-verdicts/PR-2016.json` today contains ONLY the final APPROVED verdict — keys are mode, recorded_at, recorded_by, reviewed_branch, reviewed_sha, summary, verdict, and no rounds, history or previous. The three CHANGES REQUESTED rounds I quoted at length this session are gone from the store.

That matters more than losing audit trail. I withdrew a scope criterion from BUG-1310 tonight, and the entire justification was that findings 1 across rounds 1, 2 and 3 named DIFFERENT sites each time — glab_stderr_is_transient, then git_ops/forge/compete/overlay, then remote_create/cache/git_ops-autostash — which is what proved the criterion unbounded rather than merely unmet. That evidence no longer exists anywhere in the substrate. It survives in my session transcript and in the comment I wrote onto the spec, both of which are prose I happened to write down. A decision to narrow acceptance is exactly the kind of thing someone will want to audit later, and it is currently not reconstructible.

So STORY-1391's first step is not preparatory work for the detection feature. It is the thing that makes tonight's scope decision defensible, and I would raise its priority on that basis alone.

ON YOUR THREE DESIGN CONSTRAINTS. All three are right and the second is the one I would have got wrong. TASK-1289 went five rounds and needed a design decision; a round-count threshold would have parked it automatically and produced a worse outcome than the five rounds did. Pointing the signal at the brief rather than the implementer is also right and is the whole value — the escalating-firmness failure mode is real and I performed it myself tonight before you named it.

ON THE ENTRIES SHIPPING WITHOUT SPEC IDS. Agreed and correct. Land both once amended; you have my ratification and you do not need a second pass from me on the wording.
